text: SOUTH KOREA'S LEVERAGE FEVER: WHY SO MANY PEOPLE BORROW TO INVEST English translation of the provided Vietnamese video transcript When
people think of South Korea, they often think of kimchi, romantic dramas, and youthful-looking oppas. But there is another issue that
has become an increasingly serious headache: more and more people believe that investing is no longer about building wealth slowly over
time. Instead, they see it as the quickest way to transform their lives. Stocks, cryptocurrencies, real estate—anything with the potential
to rise in price attracts people eager to jump in. And what makes this game so much more dangerous is margin
or, more simply, borrowed money used for investing. The consequences became clear in early 2026, when South Korea's KOSPI index plunged
by more than 18% in just a few days, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars off the market—one of its
sharpest declines in years. What stood out, however, was that many investors were using extremely high leverage. Some securities firms even
had to temporarily suspend margin lending because they had reached their lending limits. But why did this happen in a market
that is far from an emerging one? South Korea is one of Asia's largest economies. It has weathered numerous financial crises
and its people are famous for being competitive and disciplined in their work. So why are so many people willing to
borrow money to bet on the market? And why has leverage become so popular? That's what we're going to explore in
today's video. I'm Nheo, and this is the story of South Korea's leverage fever. First, we need to understand what leverage
or margin trading—actually is. Let's have a quick refresher. Margin trading, simply put, means borrowing money from a brokerage to
buy additional shares. Say you have 100 million Vietnamese dong, and the brokerage lends you another 100 million. Instead of buying
100 million dong worth of stocks, you can now buy 200 million dong worth. If the share price rises by
10%, you make about 20 million dong rather than 10 million. That's the basic idea. But borrowing money does not guarantee
that the market will rise. If the shares fall by 10%, your loss is also doubled. Meanwhile, you still have to
repay the loan, along with all the interest. In a way, margin trading is like fitting a racing engine to your
investment portfolio. If you're heading in the right direction, it's fantastic. But one sharp turn can send you flying off the
track. And the most dangerous part is something called a margin call. When the value of the assets in your account
falls below the required safety threshold, the brokerage demands that you deposit more money. If you cannot do so in time
the firm has the right to sell your shares to recover its loan, regardless of whether the price is favorable or
terrible at that moment. Here's where things usually go wrong. During a market crash, tens of thousands of people can receive
margin calls at once. They all sell, which pushes prices down even further. As prices fall, more people receive margin calls
triggering yet another round of selling. Imagine a line of people standing on a staircase. All it takes is for one
person to fall, and many of the people behind them may tumble too. And that is essentially what happened in South
Korea this year. But the roots of this crash lie in the way an entire generation has come to view investing
and getting rich. South Korea currently has one of the highest household-debt ratios in the world. Over the past two decades
household debt has continued to grow and is now equivalent to almost the country's entire GDP. By the end of 2025
total household credit was approaching 2,000 trillion won—an enormous amount. What is particularly important is that a large share
of this debt is connected to housing. South Korea has a rather unusual rental system called jeonse. Instead of paying
rent every month, a tenant gives the landlord a very large lump-sum deposit. In many cases, that deposit can be worth
as much as half the value of the home. In return, the tenant can live there for several years without paying
monthly rent. It sounds reasonable, but there is a problem: the upfront payment is huge. To rent a place, you already
need a substantial amount of money. When interest rates were low, this arrangement could work quite well. Money was cheap. Landlords
could invest the deposits, while tenants did not have to make monthly rent payments. Everybody seemed happy. But when interest rates
rose, many landlords began struggling to return those deposits when leases expired. And the people who felt the pressure first were
often the tenants. If you're young, the situation is even harder. The employment rate among young people is considerably lower than
in many other developed economies. Many work on short-term contracts, part-time schedules, or in otherwise unstable jobs. As a result, their
incomes rise very slowly, while living costs and asset prices keep climbing. That creates a widespread feeling among young South Koreans
even if you study hard, get a decent education, and work diligently, the life your parents' generation achieved seems to be
moving further and further out of reach. Buying a house is harder. Building wealth is harder. And the gap just keeps
widening. Against that backdrop, financial markets start to look extremely attractive. It isn't simply that people want to get rich quickly
Many feel that they don't have many other choices. If wages grow more slowly than asset prices, working hard no longer
seems like enough. You start looking for other paths. The stock market begins to look like a shortcut, and margin trading
is like being handed a faster motorcycle to take down that shortcut. But greater speed also means greater risk. Young South
Koreans have a telling way of describing this feeling: the sense of being left behind. Everything around them seems to
be accelerating—home prices, asset prices, and the wealth of people who already own assets—while they themselves remain stuck in
the same place. When that feeling spreads across an entire generation, it begins to shape financial decisions. People jump into the
market after reading a few investment books, or simply because they feel that time is chasing them. House prices are chasing
them. Living expenses are chasing them. And if they don't run faster, the gap will only get bigger. But that is
only half the story. The other half lies in the structure of South Korea's stock market. One unusual feature of the
South Korean market is the enormous role played by individual investors. In many developed markets, much of the daily trading comes
from investment funds, banks, and large financial institutions. Retail investors are still there, of course, but they are not usually the
main force determining short-term market trends. In South Korea, however, individual investors have accounted for a large share of market turnover
for years. In 2020, they represented roughly two-thirds of trading volume. Even in 2026, their share has frequently hovered around 60
In other words, about six out of every ten trades come from individual investors. That is a very high proportion, and
it has an important consequence: when retail investors get excited, huge amounts of money can rush into the market. When they
panic, selling pressure can arrive just as quickly. The market therefore becomes especially sensitive to crowd psychology. South Koreans even have
a nickname for these individual investors: gaemi, meaning 'ants.' An ant may be tiny, but if a million ants all move
in the same direction, they can generate a surprisingly powerful force—especially when many of them are carrying financial leverage. Research
on investment behavior in South Korea has identified a number of familiar mistakes among individual investors. They are easily influenced by
the crowd. They buy because they see others buying. They experience FOMO—the fear of missing out—when a stock
starts climbing rapidly. Many also enjoy hunting for small, high-risk stocks that might rise in price very quickly. It's a bit
like buying a lottery ticket and hoping to hit the jackpot. Another common tendency is selling profitable investments too early while
holding on to losing ones, hoping the price will eventually recover. This is a well-known phenomenon in behavioral finance, and it
is certainly not unique to South Korea. Investors around the world make the same mistakes. But in South Korea, those tendencies
become more extreme when margin trading enters the picture, because the people using margin are often among the most active traders
According to research by the Korea Capital Market Institute, or KCMI, margin users make up only a small proportion of individual
investors, yet they generate a disproportionately large number of trades. They trade more frequently, prefer more volatile stocks, hold more concentrated
portfolios, and accept higher levels of risk. In other words, they are the people pressing down hardest on the accelerator. The
problem is that their cars are running on borrowed money. When the market is doing well, everything seems fine. They may
make more money than everyone else. But when the market crashes, they tend to be among the first to get into
trouble—and the consequences can be especially devastating. Ironically, once you add up all the costs—trading fees, margin interest, and
investment losses—this group's results are often no better than those of ordinary investors. In many cases, they are actually worse
They take greater risks, experience more stress, and trade more often, yet the final outcome is not necessarily any better. That
is one of the greatest paradoxes of South Korea's margin-trading fever. So why are so many South Korean investors willing to
make such enormous bets? There are several reasons. The first is the pressure to accumulate wealth. As we discussed earlier, when
house prices rise too quickly and the traditional path of saving becomes increasingly unrealistic, people naturally start looking for alternatives
The stock market is one of the few places where ordinary people can still feel that they have a chance to
change their lives. All you need is a smartphone, a trading account, and a few taps to enter the game. For
many young people, this feels almost like their last realistic opportunity to close the wealth gap. But, as we've already said
big opportunities often come with big risks. With margin trading, those risks become even larger: gains can be bigger, but losses
can come much faster. The second underlying factor is a famous concept called the 'Korea discount.' Investors use this term to
describe the tendency for South Korean stocks to trade at lower valuations than comparable businesses in other developed countries. Part of
the explanation lies in the structure of South Korea's family-controlled conglomerates, known as chaebols. Another part comes from longstanding controversies over
the rights of minority shareholders. What matters here is that many investors believe this discount exists. And if people don't believe
the market will adequately reward them for holding stocks over the long term, they become more inclined to chase profits from
shorter market swings. The third factor is short selling. In theory, short selling is a perfectly normal tool in financial markets
It helps identify irrational prices and limits the extent to which stocks become overvalued. But in the eyes of many South
Korean retail investors, short selling is a game played by large institutions, especially foreign funds. Years of scandals involving short-selling practices
have only deepened that suspicion. And when trust in the fairness of the market declines, people become less interested in playing
the long game. They want to make money quickly before they become the people someone else profits from. Finally, and perhaps
most importantly, investing has simply become too easy. Never before in history has betting on the market been so convenient
In the past, if you wanted to trade stocks, you had to call a broker, wait for confirmation, and pay substantial
fees. Now everything is right there on your phone. Buying takes seconds. Selling takes seconds. On top of that, financial content
is everywhere: analysis videos, livestreams, online communities, forums, news reports, recommendations, and predictions. Every day, people are repeatedly told that there
is another opportunity in the market. This stock is about to surge! A new trend is forming! Another rally is coming
everyone! When all these things come together, the market starts looking more like a social network than a place to invest
Everyone watches price charts, refreshes the news, and follows the crowd's reactions. The more people react, the more people trade. The
entire system has made investing so frictionless that placing a buy order is almost as easy as clicking 'like.' And when
making a trade becomes that easy, the number of bad decisions tends to rise as well. Put those four factors together
and you get a very unusual environment. On one side, there is the pressure to make money fast. On the other
there is the feeling that the rules of the game are not entirely fair. In the middle, there are countless financial
tools promising to help people even the odds. When those conditions exist at the same time, the market inevitably creates products
to satisfy that demand. A striking example is the CFD scandal of 2023. CFD stands for 'contract for difference.' To put
it simply, a CFD allows you to speculate on whether an asset's price will go up or down without actually owning
the underlying asset. Like many other speculative products, CFDs often come with substantial leverage. And that can be extremely dangerous. According
to South Korean financial regulators, most of the people participating in CFD trading were actually individual investors. But in trading data
many of their transactions were recorded under the names of institutions or foreign investors. This distorted the market. Looking at
the data, it became difficult to tell who was actually buying, who was selling, and who was ultimately carrying the risk
When the scandal came to light, regulators responded in the familiar way: they introduced new rules, raised margin requirements, tightened eligibility
standards, and stepped up supervision. But those measures only addressed the symptoms. The underlying desire to speculate remained. Close one door
and people start looking for another. As CFDs came under tighter restrictions, money flowed into other leveraged products. Some of it
moved into overseas markets; some went into financial instruments that were more complicated and harder to supervise. By the end of
2024, South Korean individual investors had built up substantial holdings of foreign stocks. Among their investments, higher-risk products were becoming increasingly
common, including forms of leverage that were already restricted or tightly controlled at home. In other words, when people couldn't play
the game in their own backyard, they went looking for another field. This is why some experts compare speculation to flowing
water. You can block one stream, but the water will find another route. The more firmly you block it, the more
it tries to squeeze through smaller gaps. Sometimes it ends up somewhere even harder to control than where it started. So
banning one financial product does not necessarily eliminate the demand for speculation. It may simply push that demand into another form
one that is farther away, more complicated, and less visible. But everything we've discussed does not mean that South Koreans are
inherently greedy or obsessed with getting rich quickly. When an entire system puts pressure on people every day, choices that look
irrational to outsiders can make perfect sense to the people facing those pressures. Imagine you're a 28-year-old South Korean. Your job
isn't stable. Your contract gets renewed one year at a time, and you have no idea what the future holds. Meanwhile
housing prices are so high that you have no idea when you'll ever be able to afford a home. Every
day, you open your phone and see the stock market rising. People are constantly showing off their profits. Stories about ordinary
people becoming rich are everywhere. In those circumstances, staying on the sidelines is not easy. The scariest thing is not margin
trading itself. It's the reasons people turn to margin trading in the first place. If a generation grows up feeling that
working hard may not be enough to live comfortably, that saving for years may still not buy them a decent home
and that following the old rules will only leave them further behind, then the search for riskier options becomes almost inevitable
It isn't necessarily greed. It's a sense of helplessness, a fear of falling behind, and a belief that if you don't
speed up, you'll never catch up. And here's the irony: in the short term, the market often rewards exactly that way
of thinking. Every time the market falls and then rebounds, leveraged investors feel vindicated. They look at the profits in their
accounts and think, 'See? I was right! I'm amazing at investing. Next time, I should go even bigger.' This is one
of the market's most dangerous traps: it makes people confuse luck with skill. Winning once doesn't make you a stock-market genius
It may simply mean that you happened to be in the right place during favorable market conditions. One or two successful
trades can feel great. But it may only take a few bad ones to wipe out those gains. The debt remains
interest keeps accumulating, and time is rarely on the side of someone using leverage. At its core, this is still one
of the consequences of asset prices rising faster than incomes for a long period. Debt grows year after year. Asset prices
outpace wages. Cheap money sticks around for too long. Capital continuously flows into riskier assets. Throughout that process, many people convince
themselves that they will be the ones who manage to get out before everything goes wrong. That same belief has
appeared in almost every speculative bubble in history. And very often, it is exactly that belief that helps bring everything crashing
down. So when will South Koreans realize what's happening and walk away from this game? Actually, I think many of them
already understand the risks. But when they will step away is another question, and we don't really know the answer yet
As 2026 unfolds, South Korea's stock market continues to experience intense volatility. On one side, foreign investors keep withdrawing capital. On
the other, individual investors continue buying with determination. People have very different views about where the market is heading. Some believe
that stocks are now undervalued and that the future still looks promising. Some are even continuing to borrow money to invest
convinced that the next rebound is just around the corner. And who knows? Maybe this time they'll be right. Of course
the optimistic scenario is entirely possible. South Korea is still home to some of the world's leading companies. It has a
powerful semiconductor industry, a role in AI, and strong potential drivers of long-term growth. If conditions develop favorably, the market could
absolutely resume its upward climb after this correction. But opportunity always comes with risk. Leverage remains extremely high. Household debt is
still among the highest in the world. Meanwhile, the real economy is recovering more slowly than many had hoped. When a
financial system is loaded with leverage, every shock becomes much more dangerous. It could be a change in global interest rates
a geopolitical crisis, an unexpected development in the semiconductor industry, or simply a sudden shift in market sentiment. Perhaps the most
important question to watch over the coming years is this: can South Korea find a way to help its younger generation
build wealth without forcing them to take bigger and bigger gambles? Thank you for watching. Don't forget to subscribe so you won't miss any future videos
